title: CuTe DSL Limitations Overview
critical_patterns: Use conditional logic instead of early exits in loops
Define variables before entering control flow blocks
Maintain type stability within control flow
Allocate memory in host code, pass to kernel
Manually handle broadcasting in kernel logic
Use cute.printf() for debugging within kernels
Use preprocessor=True for full feature support
constraints: No early exit from loops (break, continue, return, pass)
Variables defined in control flow are not available outside
Cannot change variable types in control flow
No exceptions in dynamic control flow
Cannot mix compile-time and runtime values
Limited Python object support in kernels
No dynamic memory allocation in kernels
Limited type inference in some cases
Shared memory limits per block vary by architecture
Maximum threads per block is architecture dependent
Limited Python debugging tools inside kernels
JIT compilation overhead on first call
Not supported in kernels: Classes, OOP, async/await, etc.
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL is a powerful tool for writing GPU kernels but comes with several limitations designed to ensure safety, predictability, and performance. Key limitations include restrictions on dynamic control flow, such as the prohibition of early exits like break, continue, and return within loops. Variables defined within control flow blocks are not accessible outside, and type changes within control flow are not allowed to maintain type stability. Compile-time and runtime values cannot be mixed, necessitating the use of range_constexpr() for compile-time loops. Memory allocation must be handled in host code, as dynamic allocation is not supported within kernels. The type system requires explicit annotations in some cases, and automatic broadcasting is not available, requiring manual handling of operations. Preprocessor mode limitations suggest using preprocessor=True for full feature support, as tracing mode has severe limitations like branch collapse and loop unrolling. Architecture-specific constraints include tensor core requirements and shared memory limits, which vary across GPU architectures. Debugging is limited, with standard Python tools unavailable inside kernels, necessitating the use of cute.printf() for debugging. Performance considerations include JIT compilation overhead on the first call and potential slowdowns with dynamic shapes. Language features not supported in kernels include classes, OOP features, async/await, and others. Best practices involve starting simple, using default settings, validating early, and profiling before optimizing. When encountering limitations, consult documentation, simplify code, seek help, or consider alternative tools like raw CUDA or Triton.
